en: The Sūtra on the Death of the Brahmin’s Son and the Inseparable Love and Remembrance, translated by the Parthian śramaṇa An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
In that garden, there was once a certain brahmin whose son had passed away; his love for him was so profound that he could not bear to be parted from him.

Because of his death, the father could neither eat nor drink, nor would he put on clothes or apply perfumes; he went only to the cemetery to weep, and as he wept, he remembered his son while holding him in his arms.
Thereupon, that brahmin wandered about until he reached the place where the Blessed One was; having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings, the brahmin withdrew and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One said:
"For what reason?
Have your faculties, O Brahmin, not been constantly composed?"
“Gautama! How should my faculty of mind be composed?
I have a son who has passed away, and my love for him does not leave me.”

When he passed away, I could not eat, I could not drink, I did not put on clothes, and I did not apply perfumes; I merely stayed at home weeping, and while weeping, I remembered him as he lay upon my lap.
"So it is, so it is, brahmin! O brahmin!"
"When affection has arisen, there is then grief, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness.
"How could this be so, Gautama?
Is it truly thus?"
"Once craving has arisen, will there not be sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure?
"Indeed, Gautama!
Once craving has arisen, there will be joy and affectionate longing."
A second and a third time, the World-Honored One said to that brahmin: "So it is,
so it is, brahmin!"
“O Brahmin! When craving arises, there is sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and unhappiness.
This was said a second and a third time. Then that Brahmin addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“How is this, Gautama? Could it be so?
Once craving has arisen, does there not arise sorrow, grief, and dissatisfaction?”
"O Gautama! Once craving has arisen, there is only joy and affectionate attachment.
Thereupon, having heard what the Blessed One had said, that brahmin neither rejoiced nor spoke in disapproval.
Finding neither pleasure nor satisfaction, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, there were various performers playing outside the gate of Jetavana. Seeing the performers playing outside the gate of Jetavana from afar, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Those who are wise in this world are the most excellent; whatever I have intended to discuss with the ascetic Gautama, I shall now explain it all to these performers."
Thereupon, that brahmin went to where those performers were; having arrived, he recounted to those performers everything that had been discussed with the World-Honored One.
When he had spoken thus, those performers replied to that brahmin, saying:
"O brahmin! How could this be so?"
"Once craving has arisen, does there then follow sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
and unhappiness? "Brahmin,
once craving has arisen, there will instead be joy and affectionate attachment."
Thereupon, that brahmin thought to himself, "The words of these performers are the same as ours.
Having turned his head away, he immediately departed.
What he discussed was widely heard and gradually reached the royal palace.
When King Prasenajit heard it, [he learned that] the śramaṇa Gautama had spoken thus:
"Once craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness."
Having heard this, King Prasenajit said to Queen Mallikā: "Mallikā!
I have heard that the ascetic Gautama has spoken thus:"
"Once craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness. "So it is, so it is,
Great King!"
"When craving has arisen, there is then suffering, grief, lamentation, and unhappiness. "This, Mallikā!
I have heard from your teacher that it is so for the disciple as well."
"O Mālikā! That ascetic Gautama is your teacher, yet now you speak these words:
'When craving arises, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure.'"
“Great King! If you do not believe what I have said, you may go yourself or send a messenger.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit addressed the brahmin Nāḷijangha, saying:
"Nalijangha! Go to where that ascetic Gautama is.
Upon arrival, inquire after the ascetic Gautama in my name with boundless greetings, asking: 'Are you at ease, well, light of limb, and strong?'"
He spoke these words:
"O Gautama! King Prasenajit sends his greetings to you in immeasurable measure; he asks whether you are at ease, light of limb, and full of strength."
"Truly, Śramaṇa Gautama!
You have said this:
'When craving arises, do sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure not come into being?'"
"Nārāyaṇa! If that śramaṇa Gautama should speak thus, you should properly receive, uphold, recite, and study it. Why is this?"
"He does not speak falsely.

Having quickly received King Prasenajit’s instruction, that Brahmin Nāḷijangha went to where the Blessed One was. Upon arrival, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; having exchanged greetings, he withdrew and sat to one side.
Having sat down to one side, the brahmin Nāḷijangha addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“O Gautama! King Prasenajit sends his greetings;
he asks whether you are at ease, well, and free from fatigue, and whether you possess strength.”
"Is it true, Nāḷiyagga, that the ascetic Gautama has said:
'When craving arises, there is then sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness'? "It is so, Nāḷiyagga!"
I shall ask you a question; answer it according to your ability.
What do you think, Nāḷiyagga?
Suppose there is a man whose mother has passed away. After her death, she becomes deranged in mind and wanders about naked, without clothing, saying these words:
"I do not see my mother; I do not see my mother.
O Brahmin, you should know this: once craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness.

In this way, when a father, elder brother, sister, or wife passes away, once that wife has passed away, his mind becomes deranged; he goes about naked, wearing no clothes, following after her, saying:
"I do not see my father or my wife."
"O brāhmaṇa! You should know that once this craving has arisen, there is grief, lamentation, suffering, and dissatisfaction. O brāhmaṇa!"

Once there was a man whose wife returned to her home; his relatives wished to seize her and give her to another. When that woman heard it, she thought, "My relatives wish to take me and give me to another."
Having heard this, the woman quickly ran back.
Upon reaching her husband, she said to him:
"You should know, my relatives wish to give me away to another."
"What you ought to do, you shall now do.
Thereupon, that man fashioned an extremely sharp blade, took his wife by the hand, and returned into the house, saying these words:
"We must go together; we must go together."
"To take that woman's life is to take one's own life as well. O brāhmaṇa!
You should know that once this craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure."

Then, having heard what the Blessed One had said, the brahmin Nāḷiyagiri received it well and, having memorized and practiced it, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One, and departed from the Blessed One’s presence to return to King Prasenajit.
Having arrived, he addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
"It is indeed so, Great King!
That śramaṇa Gautama makes this statement:"
“When craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and unhappiness.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit said to Lady Mallikā:
“It is truly so, Mallikā!”
"That ascetic Gautama says:
'When craving arises, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and dissatisfaction.
Therefore, Great King!"
I further asked the King, "I shall repay you according to my ability.
What do you think, Great King?
Do you love the general Vairūḍaka?"
“Mallikā! I love that general Bhūriśravas.
“Great King! [she replied.]
“Does that general Bhūriśravas experience suffering, grief, distress, and dissatisfaction due to decay and change?
“Mallikā! When General Bhūriśravas undergoes decay and change, he indeed experiences grief, suffering, and dissatisfaction.”
“Great King! You should know this:
once craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure.
What do you think, Great King?”
Do you love the great general Bhadraka, do you love the great elephant Bhadradanta, do you love the woman Vāsitthī, do you love the lady Vāsabhakhattiyā, and do you love the people of Kāsi?
“Mallikā, I love the people of Kāśī and Kosala.
“Great King! [she replied.]
"Are the people of Kāśi and Kosala also subject to decay and change, giving rise to suffering, grief, distress, and discontent?
"This is so, Mallikā!"
"Those who indulge themselves in the fivefold sensual pleasures all do so because of the people of Kāśi and Kosala.
This, Mallikā!
Since the people of Kāśi are ruined and transformed, my life is not whole; how much more so would suffering, grief, distress, and displeasure not arise?"
“O Great King! You should know that once this craving has arisen, there is suffering, grief, lamentation, and dissatisfaction.
What do you think, Great King?”
"Now, do you not pity me? "Mallikā!
I too pity you."
“Great King! This wife of mine is also subject to decay and change; how could one not give rise to suffering, grief, distress, and displeasure? “You, Mallikā!”
"When there is decay and change, I too shall experience sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure.
"In this way, Great King,
you should know that once craving has arisen, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and displeasure."
“Mallikā! From this day forward, because of this matter, that ascetic Gautama shall be my teacher, and I shall be his disciple.”
"O Mallikā!

I now take refuge in that Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I shall maintain the status of an upāsaka toward that Blessed One; from this day forward, I abstain from taking life. I now take refuge in the Buddha."
When this was said, King Prasenajit heard from afar what the World-Honored One had spoken; he rejoiced and was filled with delight.
This concludes the Discourse on the Death of the Brahmin’s Son and the Enduring Love that Does Not Depart.
